conventions.convention: Dimension d≥1; time starts at zero; x_k is F_k-measurable, G_k is F_{k+1}-measurable, and stepsizes are deterministic and positive. Independence across iterations is not assumed.

Conditional expectations are coordinatewise almost-sure classes under AC; coordinates used in conditional moments are square-integrable. Vector conditional variance is the sum of coordinate conditional variances, distinct from the conditional second moment.
The almost-supermartingale lemma requires deterministic nonnegative summable a_k,c_k and nonnegative F_k-measurable integrable b_k; X_k must be nonnegative, adapted and integrable at every time.
Strong convexity on C uses the strong-Jensen inequality with subtraction (μ/2)t(1−t)||x−y||²; differentiability is on an open convex ambient domain, permitting boundary points of C.
P_C is the unique Euclidean nearest-point map for nonempty closed convex C; projected SGD forms y_k=x_k−α_kG_k and then x_{k+1}=P_C(y_k).
The nonconvex output index is independent and uniform on {0,…,N−1}, selected on a finite product extension; its expected squared gradient equals the uniform average over those iterates.

load_bearing.statement: For deterministic α_k>0, x_{k+1}=x_k−α_kG_k. Conditional unbiasedness means E[G_k|F_k]=∇f(x_k); conditional bias means E[G_k|F_k]=∇f(x_k)+b_k. Vector conditional second moment equals the squared conditional mean plus the sum of coordinate conditional variances.

Assume AC. For nonnegative adapted integrable X_k, deterministic nonnegative summable a_k,c_k, and nonnegative F_k-measurable integrable b_k, if E[X_{k+1}|F_k]≤(1+a_k)X_k−b_k+c_k almost surely for every k, then X_k converges almost surely to a finite nonnegative random variable and Σb_k<∞ almost surely.

Let U⊆R^d be open and convex, C⊆U convex, and f:U→R differentiable. If f restricted to C satisfies the μ-strong-Jensen inequality for μ>0, then f(y)≥f(x)+⟨∇f(x),y−x⟩+(μ/2)||y−x||² and ⟨∇f(x)−∇f(y),x−y⟩≥μ||x−y||² for all x,y∈C.
For nonempty closed convex C⊆R^d and x_0∈C, form y_k=x_k−α_kG_k and set x_{k+1}=P_C(y_k), where P_C is the unique nearest-point map.

Euclidean norm squares, symmetry, bilinearity and scalar specialization.
Inner-product bounds, triangle inequalities and elementary square estimates.
Convex objective-gap estimates and optimality when the gradient vanishes.

Mean-value derivation of 1+t≤exp(t) for t≥0.
Bounding products by exp(Σa_k).
Derivation of the exponential product bound.
Converting finite products of exponentials into exponentials of finite sums.
